title: Schleiermacher
hookLine: religion as the feeling of absolute dependence

lines: NAME ONE THING YOU MADE YOURSELF.
RELIGION IS FINISHED, HIS FRIENDS SAID.
IT BEGINS IN FEELING, HE SAID.
cards: A short experiment. Name one thing in this minute that you made yourself. The breath you just took came without asking.
Your heartbeat started before you knew your own name. The floor under you, the light in the room, the language you're thinking in: all handed to you.

Friedrich Schleiermacher, a German preacher and professor, pointed at that kind of givenness. He wrote a book for educated friends who thought religion was finished, a pile of old rules and stale arguments.
They were looking in the wrong place, he said. Religion begins deeper down, in a kind of feeling.

teach.b: In his book The Christian Faith, Schleiermacher names the heart of religion in one phrase, usually given in English as the feeling of absolute dependence.
Feeling: not a mood like happy or sad, but an awareness underneath the moods, a sense of where you stand.
Dependence: we know the partial kind all the time. You depend on the bus, a paycheck, a friend, and you push back on the world a little: you choose, you act, you change things. That freedom is real.
But in one relation, he says, the push only goes one way. Your whole self, your freedom included, comes from somewhere you didn't make.
That's absolute dependence, and the word God, for him, names the one we depend on in that way. The Bible has its own words for it.

teach.h: IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE
teach.b: Paul, speaking in Athens, says of God: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being." A psalm pictures every creature waiting on God: "These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season."
Some said he turned faith into a mood, moving the center from God speaking to humans feeling; Karl Barth, whom this path meets again soon, argued with him hard.
His defenders answer that he meant something steadier: the plain fact of being held, finally noticed. Christians still argue about where he leads.
But his question stays a fair one: before any argument, what is it like to be a creature?

how: Christians who draw on Schleiermacher often describe prayer less as asking and more as resting in awareness of God as the source of all things; his thought is studied in Protestant seminaries and debated across the churches.

o: a German hymn style sung in four-part harmony
a German theologian: religion begins in feeling
a German reformer who nailed up ninety-five theses

p: in him we live, and move

s: for Schleiermacher, "feeling" meant a passing mood
he meant an awareness under every mood: the sense of being wholly dependent.
Paul told the Athenians, "in him we live, and move, and have our being"
Acts 17:28, from Paul's speech in Athens.
critics, Karl Barth among them, said he moved the center from God speaking to humans feeling.

games.q: you're Schleiermacher. your educated friends say religion is finished: old rules, stale arguments. how do you answer them?
o: say religion begins before rules and arguments, in a feeling.
games.why: he told them they were looking in the wrong place: religion begins in the feeling of absolute dependence, a whole life received.

practice: Notice what's holding you right now: the floor under you, the air coming in unasked, your heart keeping time on its own, then wider, the people who grew your food and taught you to read, until the list runs past what you can name.
You don't have to call it anything. If you pray, you can rest in Paul's line: in him we live, and move, and have our being.

wordCard.voice: Schleiermacher. The German theologian who said religion begins in a feeling: the sense of being utterly dependent, a whole life received.

orig.note: Greek, Acts 17:28: we live — "in him we live, and move, and have our being."

carryVoice: Your line: entirely held. Not one breath of it made by you. See you tomorrow.
